prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

THE NIGHT THAT LORCA COMES SHALL BE A STRANGE NIGHT IN THE SOUTH, IT SHALL BE THE TIME WHEN NEGROES LEAVE THE SOUTH FOREVER, GREEN TRAINS SHALL ARRIVE FROM RED PLANET MARS CRACKLING BLUENESS SHALL SEND TOOTH-COVERED CARS FOR THEM TO LEAVE IN, TO GO INTO THE NORTH FOREVER, AND I SEE MY LITTLE GIRL MOTHER AGAIN WITH HER CROSS THAT IS NOT BURNING, HER SKIRTS OF BLACK, OF ALL COLORS, HER AURA OF FAMILIARITY. THE SOUTH SHALL WEEP BITTER TEARS TO NO AVAIL, THE NEGROES HAVE GONE INTO CRACKLING BLUENESS. CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL ARRIVE WITH THE BOSTON COMMONS, TO TAKE ELISSI LANDI NORTH, CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL BE LAYING ON BOSTON COMMONS, ELISSI LANDI SHALL FEEL ALIVE AGAIN. I SHALL CALL HER NAME AS SHE STEPS ON TO THE BOSTON COMMONS, AND FLIES NORTH FOREVER, LINCOLN SHALL BE THERE, TO SEE THEM LEAVE THE SOUTH FOREVER, ELISSI LANDI, SHE WILL BE GREEN. THE WHITE SOUTH SHALL GATHER AT PRESERVATION HALL.

prompts.L3:

- Lorca’s arrival marks a strange, transformative night when Black people leave the South forever.
- Surreal green trains and tooth-covered cars from Mars carry them north into a crackling blueness.
- The speaker envisions reuniting with a familiar maternal figure whose cross is no longer burning.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem imagines Black people’s permanent exodus from the American South through surreal, prophetic imagery involving Lorca, Mars, Crispus Attucks, Lincoln, and the speaker’s mother. Their departure becomes a vision of liberation and renewal, leaving the white South to mourn while the displaced reclaim life, history, and freedom in the North.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: THE, NIGHT, THAT

outputs.L1:
The night Lorca comes shall be a strange night in the South. It shall be the time when Negroes leave the South forever. Green trains shall arrive from the red planet Mars, and crackling blueness shall send tooth-covered cars to carry them north forever.

I shall see my little-girl mother again, bearing her cross that is not burning, wearing her skirts of black—of all colors—and surrounded by her aura of familiarity. The South shall weep bitter tears, but to no avail: the Negroes have gone into crackling blueness.

Crispus Attucks shall arrive with the Boston Commons to take Elissi Landi north. Crispus Attucks shall lie upon the Boston Commons, and Elissi Landi shall feel alive again. I shall call her name as she steps onto the Boston Commons and flies north forever.

Lincoln shall be there to see them leave the South forever. Elissi Landi—she will be green. The white South shall gather at Preservation Hall.
outputs.L2:
A peculiar night will descend upon the South when Lorca arrives. It will mark the moment when Negroes abandon the region for good. Green trains will come from the red world of Mars, while a crackling blue force dispatches tooth-covered cars to carry them permanently northward. Once more, I will behold my little-girl mother, wearing her unburning cross and skirts both black and every color, surrounded by an aura I recognize.

The South will cry helpless, bitter tears, but the Negroes will already have vanished into the crackling blue. Crispus Attucks will appear together with the Boston Commons and bring Elissi Landi north. As Attucks lies upon the Commons, Elissi Landi will feel restored to life. I will cry out her name when she enters the Boston Commons and flies north forever. Lincoln will stand there, watching them depart the South for the last time. Elissi Landi will be green. Meanwhile, the white South will assemble at Preservation Hall.
outputs.L3:
Lorca’s arrival signals the beginning of a strange and transformative night: a moment when Black people leave the South behind forever. Their migration unfolds through surreal imagery. Green trains and automobiles from Mars, covered in teeth, carry them northward into a vivid, crackling blueness that suggests both uncertainty and liberation.

Amid this exodus, the speaker imagines being reunited with a familiar maternal figure. Her cross, once associated with violence and suffering, is no longer burning, suggesting the possibility of safety, healing, and release from the South’s racist terror. Historical and symbolic figures also witness the departure: Crispus Attucks, an early martyr of the American Revolution, and Abraham Lincoln observe the revival of Elissa Landi and her journey north.

As the travelers escape, the South itself seems to mourn their loss. Yet the white South responds differently, gathering at Preservation Hall as though attempting to preserve its own traditions and version of history. The scene therefore combines grief, freedom, memory, and surreal transformation, presenting the northward migration as both a departure from oppression and the beginning of a radically new existence.
outputs.L4:
The poem envisions a permanent exodus of Black people from the American South, transforming the historical Great Migration into a surreal and prophetic act of collective liberation. Rather than presenting departure as an ordinary movement from one region to another, the speaker imagines it on a cosmic scale. Figures such as Federico García Lorca, Crispus Attucks, and Abraham Lincoln appear alongside Mars and the speaker’s mother, collapsing distinctions between past and present, history and myth, the personal and the universal. Through these unexpected juxtapositions, the poem suggests that Black suffering and resistance belong not only to American history but also to a larger human struggle against violence, oppression, and exile.

Crispus Attucks evokes the long history of Black sacrifice in the United States, while Lincoln recalls emancipation and its unfulfilled promises. Lorca, a poet associated with political violence, marginalization, and artistic freedom, broadens the poem’s vision beyond America. Mars introduces both war and the possibility of another world, making the migration seem almost planetary: if freedom cannot be achieved within the existing social order, the oppressed may have to imagine an entirely new place in which to live. The speaker’s mother grounds these grand historical and cosmic references in intimate experience. Her presence reminds the reader that migration is not merely an abstract political event; it is lived through families, memories, grief, and hope.

The departure of Black Southerners is presented as final. They do not leave in order to return to the conditions that drove them away, nor do they remain emotionally bound to a region that has exploited their labor and denied their humanity. By withdrawing their bodies, culture, creativity, and historical presence, they expose the South’s dependence on the very people it has oppressed. The white South is consequently left to mourn—not simply because people have gone, but because their departure reveals an immense moral and cultural loss. Its grief arrives too late, after generations of racism have made reconciliation impossible.

Yet the poem’s dominant movement is toward renewal rather than despair. In the North, the displaced reclaim their lives and reassert their place in history. The journey becomes an act of self-determination through which they refuse the roles imposed on them by white supremacy. Although the North is not necessarily portrayed as free from racism, it functions symbolically as a space of possibility, reinvention, and greater freedom. The migrants carry their memories and ancestors with them, turning displacement into the foundation of a new collective identity.

Ultimately, the poem transforms exile into liberation. Its surreal imagery allows the speaker to imagine a future beyond the limitations of ordinary history, while its references to national heroes, artists, planets, and family members connect political freedom with cultural memory and personal survival. Black departure becomes both a judgment on the South and a declaration of independence: those who have been denied belonging will no longer wait for acceptance, but will reclaim life, history, and freedom on their own terms.
outputs.L5:
**THE NIGHT THAT REMEMBERED**

The night that changed everything arrived without warning. No thunder announced it, no stars fell from the sky. The streets simply grew quiet, and the moon hung above the rooftops like a silver question.

Mara walked alone toward the river, carrying a letter she had been afraid to open. At the water’s edge, she finally broke the seal. Inside were only three words:

*Begin again tomorrow.*

She read them twice, then let the paper drift into the current. For the first time in years, the darkness did not frighten her. It felt gentle, almost protective—as if the night itself understood that some endings were not endings at all, but doors waiting to be opened.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an all-caps surrealist prose poem about Black people leaving the American South forever, blending Federico García Lorca, the Great Migration, Mars, Abraham Lincoln, Crispus Attucks, and Preservation Hall.
counterfactuals.output:
AT MIDNIGHT THE TRAINS GREW BLACK WINGS, AND THE SOUTH, THAT OLD IRON ORCHARD, HEARD ITS LAST GOODBYE SPOKEN THROUGH A THOUSAND STEAM WHISTLES. FAMILIES LIFTED THEIR SUITCASES LIKE BIBLES FILLED WITH RED EARTH, COTTON DUST, BIRTH CERTIFICATES, AND THE NAMES OF THE DEAD. THEY LEFT FOREVER—NORTHWARD, WESTWARD, OUTWARD—WHILE THE MOON HUNG ABOVE MISSISSIPPI LIKE A WHITE MASK CRACKED BY SONG.

CRISPUS ATTUCKS WALKED BESIDE THE TRACKS, CARRYING HIS FIRST BLOOD IN A SILVER LANTERN. ABRAHAM LINCOLN, TALL AS A BURNT PINE, STOOD AT A CROSSING WITH A BROKEN COMPASS, HIS MARBLE MOUTH FULL OF UNFINISHED PROMISES. NO ONE ASKED HIS PERMISSION. THE CHILDREN HAD ALREADY BOARDED. THE MOTHERS HAD ALREADY TURNED THEIR FACES TOWARD CHICAGO, DETROIT, HARLEM, OAKLAND—CITIES BLOOMING IN THE DARK LIKE BRASS INSTRUMENTS BENEATH DEEP WATER.

THEN MARS DESCENDED, RED AND IMMENSE, A SECOND SOUTH WITHOUT SHERIFFS OR CHAINS. ROCKETS ROSE FROM CANEFIELDS. EACH FLAME WAS AN ANCESTOR SHOUTING THROUGH THE ENGINE. ON THE MARTIAN PLAINS, BLACK HANDS PLANTED COLLARD GREENS IN CRATERS AND BUILT PORCHES UNDER TWO MOONS. THE DUST LEARNED GOSPEL. THE STARS LEARNED BLUES. GRAVITY ITSELF STEPPED ASIDE.

FAR BEHIND THEM, PRESERVATION HALL OPENED ITS DOORS, AND THE HORNS BEGAN TO PLAY SO FIERCELY THAT NEW ORLEANS FLOATED THREE INCHES ABOVE THE EARTH. TRUMPETS CALLED THE DEPARTED BY NAME; TROMBONES ROLLED LIKE GOLDEN THUNDER; A DRUM BEAT A ROAD THROUGH THE SKY. THE MUSIC FOLLOWED EVERY TRAIN AND ROCKET, CROSSED EVERY RIVER, ENTERED EVERY RED PLANET WINDOW.

BY DAWN THE SOUTH WAS AN EMPTY CHAIR BENEATH A MAGNOLIA TREE. ITS SHADOW WAITED FOR SERVANTS WHO WOULD NEVER RETURN. BUT ACROSS AMERICA, AND FARTHER STILL, BLACK CITIES TURNED THEIR LIGHTS ON—ONE BY ONE, STAR BY STAR—UNTIL THE UNIVERSE COULD NO LONGER PRETEND IT HAD INVENTED THE SUN.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an Afrofuturist prophecy in a fever-dream style where green trains and strange cars arrive from Mars to carry African Americans north, while the South mourns their departure.
counterfactuals.output:
The prophecy came sweating through the radio at midnight:

**When the moon turns copper and the rails begin to bloom,  
green trains will descend from Mars.**

Not painted green—alive green: collard-leaf green, bottle-glass green, the green of a storm deciding whether to forgive the earth. Their engines will hum old spirituals backward. Their windows will shine with the faces of ancestors who escaped by foot, by river, by prayer, now returning as conductors in silver caps.

Behind them will come strange cars with comet wheels and dashboards full of stars. They will roll through cotton fields without bending a stalk. They will stop at porches, barbershops, factory gates, church steps, and jailhouse doors.

A horn will sound.

Every Black child will hear their hidden name.

Every grandmother will find a ticket beneath her tongue.

Every father lost to a road, a war, a cell, or a wage will appear in the rearview mirror, saying, **Go north. Go farther north than the maps permit.**

Then the people will rise carrying skillets, photographs, seed jars, saxophones, unfinished degrees, and the bones of songs. They will board beneath a rain of red dust. The green trains will stretch from Alabama to orbit; the strange cars will climb the night like bright beetles.

And the South will mourn.

Courthouses will ring their bells with no hands upon them. Plantation houses will cough up ghosts. Rivers will call after those they once refused to carry. Empty kitchens will remember laughter. Highways will ache beneath the absence of tires.

The magnolias will lower their white heads.

The fields will whisper, **Who will dream us now?**

But already the travelers will be crossing into a new North—not Chicago, not Detroit, not Harlem, but a city suspended beneath the pole star, where winter is powered by drums and every tower bears a garden. There, the arrivals will build streets shaped like constellations. They will forge suns in basement furnaces. They will teach the snow to dance.

And when Mars asks what became of the people it carried away, the green trains will answer:

**They were never carried away.  
They were carried forward.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-paragraph experimental poem that mixes civil rights history, racial trauma, family memory, Catholic imagery, and science fiction. Include Lorca, Boston Common, a non-burning cross, and “crackling blueness.”
counterfactuals.output: On Boston Common my grandmother folds the March on Washington into her missal, a black-and-white weather of feet, while Lorca whispers green through the ribs of the subway and the saints turn their wounded faces toward the sirens; my father remembers hoses, dogs, the bright arithmetic of doors that would not open, remembers a non-burning cross planted in the yard like a dead antenna waiting for orders from another century; above us, the moon docks its silver parish, astronauts kneel at the rail for a wafer of oxygen, and Mary wears a helmet filled with crackling blueness; I carry our family names like contraband planets—each scar an orbit, each photograph a small emancipation—and when the future descends in its chrome chariot, speaking equality in a voice almost human, we answer with hymns, with court dates, with blood under the fingernails, with Lorca’s impossible stars, until history glitches and the children step through, baptized not in forgetting but in light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you imitate the raw, incantatory style of an avant-garde 1960s Black Arts poem, written entirely in capital letters, about a mystical final exodus from the segregated South?
counterfactuals.output:
LAST TRAIN OUT OF DIXIE

O BLACK RIVER  
O MIDNIGHT MOTHER  
ROLL YOUR DARK PSALM NORTHWARD

WE COME  
WITH COTTON IN OUR SCARS  
WITH IRON IN OUR TONGUES  
WITH THE NAMES OF THE STOLEN  
BEATING DRUMS INSIDE OUR CHESTS

NO MORE BACK DOOR  
NO MORE WHITE ONLY WATER  
NO MORE YES SIR  
NO MORE HEAD BENT  
BONE BENT  
SOUL BENT  
BENEATH THE SUN OF A SHERIFF’S STAR

BURN, OLD MAP  
BURN, RED LINE  
BURN, SIGNBOARD NAILED  
TO THE FOREHEAD OF MORNING

WE ARE LEAVING  
BUT NOT EMPTY

WE CARRY THE PORCH SONG  
THE FIELD MOAN  
THE BIBLE WITH ITS THUNDER MARGINS  
THE BISCUIT TIN  
THE MIDWIFE’S HAND  
THE BLUES KNIFE  
THE LAUGHTER THEY COULD NOT LYNCH

O TRAIN  
BLACK SERPENT OF DELIVERANCE  
EAT THE MILES  
EAT THE NIGHT  
EAT EVERY COUNTY WHERE FEAR  
WORE A CLEAN WHITE SHIRT

GRANDMOTHERS RISE IN THE WINDOWS  
FATHERS RISE FROM THE CLAY  
CHILDREN YET UNBORN  
SHAKE STARS FROM THEIR HAIR

AND THE SOUTH  
THAT OLD PHARAOH  
WAKES WITH AN EMPTY WHIP

WE CROSS  
WE CROSS  
WE CROSS

NOT INTO HEAVEN  
BUT INTO OURSELVES

AND BEHIND US  
THE COTTON FIELDS KNEEL

AND BEFORE US  
A CITY WITHOUT A MASTER  
OPENS ITS THOUSAND EYES

O FREEDOM  
DO NOT WHISPER

CALL US BY OUR WHOLE NAMES

CALL US LOUD

CALL US HOME
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a bizarre apocalyptic monologue narrated by someone envisioning their mother or daughter, Elissi Landi, joining Crispus Attucks and Lincoln on a supernatural journey north as the white South gathers at Preservation Hall.
counterfactuals.output:
I saw Elissi Landi last night—my mother, or perhaps my daughter; by then the clocks had eaten their own hands, and genealogy was only a snake deciding which end to swallow.

She stood at the edge of a black river wearing a crown of moths. Crispus Attucks waited beside her in a boat carved from a thunderbolt, his coat full of seawater and ringing bells. Lincoln held the lantern. He was taller than the ruined sky, taller than the smoke, and every time he breathed, dead telegraph wires whispered from pole to pole:

**North. North. North.**

Behind them, the white South gathered at Preservation Hall.

They came in linen and bone, in wedding veils yellowed by hurricanes, carrying portraits that had begun to sweat. The trumpets played without musicians. The piano opened its ivory mouth and confessed. From the balconies hung Spanish moss, receipts, old flags, and the pale skins of forgotten laws. Everyone waited for history to rise and tell them they had been innocent.

But history had no such intention.

Elissi looked back at me. Her face was young, then ancient, then mine.

“Are you my mother?” I called.

“Not anymore,” she said.

“Are you my daughter?”

“Not yet.”

Then Attucks struck the river with his oar, and the water split into a thousand northbound roads. Lincoln lifted the lantern, and inside its flame I saw cities kneeling beneath red snow. I saw monuments sprout legs and flee their pedestals. I saw the moon indicted by a jury of crows. Above Preservation Hall, an enormous white magnolia opened, and from its center descended—not an angel, no—but a locomotive with antlers, shrieking the names of the unremembered.

The gathering fell silent.

Elissi stepped into the boat.

“Where are you going?” I begged.

“Past the border of the map.”

“What is there?”

She smiled as the dead sometimes smile when they know the living have misunderstood everything.

“Morning,” she said.

And they went north: Attucks rowing through fire, Lincoln lighting the miles, Elissi Landi standing at the prow while the compass spun itself blind. Behind them, Preservation Hall filled with saltwater. The trumpets grew gills. The portraits screamed. The old piano floated upward through the roof and vanished among the stars.

Now the horizon is splitting.

Now the birds are flying backward into their eggs.

Now every road points north, even the roads that do not exist.

And I am still here, calling after Elissi—mother, daughter, beginning, end—while the last magnolia burns without being consumed, and the whole white South, gathered in its finery, waits for a verdict delivered in thunder.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
